subject: dsa
title: Complexity Analysis
summary: How to measure and reason about the cost of algorithms: growth rates, Big-O/Omega/Theta, analysing code, space, amortised analysis, recurrences and the Master Theorem, and what complexity means on real hardware.

lessons.title: Algorithms and counting work
lessons.summary: Count a scan with an explicit model of a basic operation.
lessons.body:
An algorithm is a precise procedure for carrying out a task. Before comparing speed, establish what inputs are valid and what answer is required. For the terminating problems in this module, a correct solution must finish and return the right answer on every valid input. Passing a few tests is evidence, not a proof of that guarantee.

## Count the work that repeats

Timings tell you how one implementation behaves on one machine. Counting operations explains how its workload changes when the input grows. Here n is the number of list items.

```python
# total([2, 3, 5]) returns 10.
def total(xs):
    s = 0
    for x in xs:
        s += x
    return s
```

This scan adds each item once. Doubling a long list roughly doubles the additions. Initialising and returning the total add fixed overhead; they do not change that linear growth.

A **cost model** states what counts as one step. A simple RAM model treats a bounded-size comparison, arithmetic operation or memory access as constant cost. Counting loop overhead changes the coefficient, but this scan remains linear. A function call also includes the work its body performs.

Python integers can grow to many digits, and comparing long strings may inspect many characters. Treating those operations as constant cost is an explicit simplification, not a property of every Python value. Real memory access and allocation also have costs the simple model omits.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Checking a guest list
> Checking each printed name once takes more work when the list grows.
>
> **How it maps:** One check per name corresponds to one addition per input item; picking up the list is fixed setup work.
>
> **Where it stops:** Human checks vary in duration. The algorithm model counts specified operations and must state which have constant cost.

## Key takeaways
- Correctness and termination come before efficiency.
- Define input size and the operation being counted.
- One pass with constant work per item has linear growth.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

questions.prompt: Which properties are required of a deterministic procedure that correctly solves a terminating task on every valid input? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every step is precisely defined, with no ambiguity
options.explanation: Correct. 'Pick a good pivot' is not an algorithm step; 'pick the middle element' is. Unambiguous steps are part of the definition.

options.text: It finishes after a finite number of steps on every valid input
options.explanation: Correct. A promised answer on every valid input requires termination on each of those inputs.

options.text: It runs in polynomial time
options.explanation: Not required. An exponential-time brute-force search is still an algorithm, just a slow one. Efficiency is how we *compare* algorithms, not what makes something one.

options.text: It produces the correct output for every valid input
options.explanation: Correct. Working on the test cases you tried is not enough; correctness means all valid inputs.

options.text: It has been implemented in a programming language
options.explanation: Not required. A precise algorithm can be described and analysed before it is implemented.

questions.workedExample: Separate correctness from speed. A valid terminating solution needs precise steps, must finish on every valid input and must return the specified result. It can still be slow, and its procedure can be described before anyone implements it.

lessons.title: Comparing every pair
lessons.summary: Count the comparisons in a duplicate check that visits each distinct pair once.
lessons.body:
Comparing each item with every other item creates much more work than scanning once. Here n is the number of list items, and equality comparisons are assumed constant cost.

## Why avoiding repeats still leaves quadratic work

```python
# has_dup([2, 3, 2]) returns True.
def has_dup(xs):
    for i in range(len(xs)):
        # Check each pair only once.
        for j in range(i + 1, len(xs)):
            if xs[i] == xs[j]:
                return True
    return False
```

Starting the inner loop after the outer position avoids comparing an item with itself and avoids checking a pair in both orders. The first item still meets every later item; later passes become progressively shorter. With no duplicates, none can exit early.

Doubling a large list roughly quadruples these comparisons: there are about twice as many items, each with about twice as many possible partners. Checking only half the full square changes the amount of work, but its growth remains quadratic.

The exact pair count is useful when budgeting comparisons, but the growth argument does not require calculating it:

```formula reference
C(n) = n(n − 1) / 2
where
C(n): the number of distinct pairs of positions, and worst-case equality checks in this function
n: the nonnegative number of list items
In words: pair each position with every different position, then halve the result because reversing a pair does not create a new pair.
```

Do not classify code by counting nested loops alone. Two consecutive full passes are linear. A full pass containing a fixed hundred checks is also linear. A nested inner range proportional to the input gives quadratic work.

For large duplicate checks, sorting makes equal values adjacent; an efficient comparison sort followed by a scan takes O(n log n) time. A hash set takes expected O(n) time under suitable hashing assumptions, using extra memory. Neither bound promises a specific runtime.

## Key takeaways
- Avoiding repeated pairs reduces work without removing quadratic growth.
- An early return helps only inputs that reach it early.
- Improving the search structure can matter more than speeding up each comparison.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

questions.prompt: A CSV validator compares every pair of rows to detect duplicates. Small test files are fast, but large mostly distinct uploads time out. Which change best addresses the source of growth?

options.text: Increase the request timeout only
options.explanation: This may let more work finish but leaves the quadratic comparison count.

lessons.title: Comparing growth rates
lessons.summary: Compare logarithmic, linear, quadratic and exponential operation counts.
lessons.body:
A growth rate describes how work changes as the input becomes larger. It is a scaling prediction, not a stopwatch reading. Here n is the item count and each counted operation has constant cost.

## Recognise the behaviour

| Growth | What creates it | Effect of a larger input |
|---|---|---|
| Constant | fixed amount of work | no input-dependent increase |
| Logarithmic | repeatedly discard a fixed fraction | doubling adds roughly one halving step |
| Linear | visit every item once | doubling roughly doubles work |
| Linear times log | linear work over logarithmically many levels | doubling costs slightly more than twice |
| Quadratic | compare all pairs | doubling roughly quadruples work |
| Exponential | explore independent binary choices | each extra choice doubles candidates |

A base-two **logarithm** is the power needed to produce a value from two. For powers of two it also counts repeated halvings down to one. Ten halvings reduce 1,024 to one; doubling that starting size adds just one halving. For other sizes, an algorithm rounds its number of steps as its stopping rule requires.

The contrast between linear, quadratic and exponential growth is worth seeing directly:

```formula essential
W_linear(n) = n
W_pairs(n) = n^2
W_subsets(n) = 2^n
where
W_linear(n): an idealised count with one operation per input item
W_pairs(n): an idealised full ordered-pair count, including self-pairs
W_subsets(n): the number of subsets of n distinct items, assuming one check per subset
n: the nonnegative item count
In words: a scan grows with the item count, all-pairs work grows with its square, and adding one binary choice doubles the number of subsets.
```

The subset model counts candidates. If checking a candidate requires scanning its contents, include that cost too.

Small test inputs can conceal an expensive growth rate. Conversely, a small fixed input may make exhaustive search entirely sensible. There is no universal item cutoff for exponential algorithms: candidate cost, pruning, hardware and the available time all matter.

## Key takeaways
- Recognise how the work changes before calculating an exact count.
- Logarithmic growth comes from reducing the remaining problem by a fixed factor.
- Growth labels help compare scaling; measurements settle practical runtime.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

options.explanation: A count model still needs operation costs and environmental assumptions.

lessons.title: What faster hardware buys
lessons.summary: Translate a hardware speedup into the input size each growth rate can handle.
lessons.body:
A faster machine can help immediately. How much larger an input it can handle in the same time depends on the algorithm's growth.

## More work budget, different input gains

Assume the new machine performs every counted operation at the same fixed speedup, with memory and other resources sufficient. This deliberately excludes changes in parallel overhead, cache behaviour or algorithm choice.

- For a linear scan, twice the work budget buys twice as many items.
- For pairwise work, twice as many items need roughly four times the budget. Input capacity grows more slowly than hardware speed.
- For a search that checks every subset at constant cost, each additional item doubles the candidate count. A doubling of machine speed therefore buys only one more item.

That last rule is additive: repeated hardware doublings add items rather than multiplying the previous item limit. A thousandfold speedup buys about ten extra binary choices under this model. It does not make an arbitrary exponential search practical.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A growing dinner party
> Serving one plate per guest and arranging a conversation between every pair scale differently.
>
> **How it maps:** Plates resemble linear work; pair meetings resemble quadratic work. Faster service buys less extra capacity when the number of relationships also grows.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real meetings can overlap. The algorithm comparison assumes a fixed counted-work model and a uniform speedup.

A lower growth rate can give a larger long-term improvement than a constant hardware speedup, but that is not a reason to dismiss hardware upgrades. Measure the current bottleneck and expected input range. A better algorithm may have extra setup or memory costs; a practical decision includes those too.

## Key takeaways
- Hardware changes the work budget under the stated model.
- Quadratic work turns a large speed gain into a smaller input gain.
- Binary-choice exhaustive search gains one item per doubling of speed.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

options.explanation: Correct. The extra budget must cover the square of the input multiplier.

options.explanation: That describes constant-cost binary-choice enumeration, not quadratic work.

options.explanation: Correct. Adding one binary choice doubles the number of subsets.

options.explanation: Hardware changes a constant factor, not the algorithm’s growth mechanism.

options.explanation: The doubled work budget can cover one extra doubling of subset count.

lessons.title: Input size and dominant terms
lessons.summary: Choose the right input measure and simplify a cost without forgetting its limits.
lessons.body:
Calling an algorithm "linear" is incomplete until you say what it is linear in.

## Choose the measure that drives the work

- For a list, n usually counts items.
- For a graph, V counts vertices and E counts edges. A traversal may need O(V + E) work; neither dimension can be dropped without a relationship between them.
- For an image, count pixels when the algorithm visits pixels. Doubling both dimensions quadruples pixel count.
- For a number, input length counts its digits or bits, rather than its numeric value.

Adding one bit approximately doubles the range of positive integers representable at that length. A primality test that tries every possible divisor up to the number's value can therefore take exponentially many iterations in the bit length. An early exit on composite inputs does not fix the prime-input worst case. Division on large integers also costs more than a single fixed-size operation.

Testing only up to the square root reduces work substantially, but remains exponential in bit length. A polynomial bound in numeric value need not be polynomial in the encoded input length; this distinction is called **pseudo-polynomial time**.

## What dominant terms tell you

An all-pairs comparison has a quadratic main term and a smaller linear correction. For large inputs, the quadratic part determines scaling. Dropping fixed multipliers and lower-order terms produces a useful growth label.

It does not produce an exact runtime or a universal winner. A simple quadratic implementation can beat a linear-times-log implementation over a small input range because of lower setup and per-step costs. The slower growth rate wins eventually under comparable fixed cost models, but the crossover must be established rather than assumed.

## Key takeaways
- Always name the input measure, including independent dimensions.
- Numeric value and encoded length can give very different complexity descriptions.
- Dominant growth predicts scaling, while constants still matter at finite sizes.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

options.text: Linear in the input size, so fast for any 64-bit number
options.explanation: The loop is linear in numeric value, while input size is bit count. Adding one input bit can roughly double the numeric range and the work of trial division through that range.

options.text: Logarithmic, because it returns as soon as it finds a divisor
options.explanation: Early exit helps for composite numbers with small factors, but when N is prime the loop runs all N - 2 times. Cost is judged on the worst case here.

options.text: Constant time, because a 64-bit number has a fixed size
options.explanation: A literally fixed finite input domain admits a constant upper bound, but that hides the huge practical cost. The question asks how work grows when bit width varies.

options.text: Linear in numeric value, exponential in bit count
options.explanation: Correct. Adding bits doubles the largest representable value. Work proportional to that value is exponential in bit count.

questions.workedExample: Measure the input in bits. A prime forces the loop to try every candidate divisor below its value. Adding bits greatly increases that value, so a linear iteration count in numeric value is exponential in bit length. Early exits on composites do not remove the prime-input worst case; large-integer division adds further cost.

options.text: The growth analysis must be wrong
options.explanation: Different fixed costs can reverse practical performance over a finite range.

options.text: Lower fixed costs can make the quadratic choice useful over that range
options.explanation: Correct. Growth describes eventual scaling, while measured finite-size costs include constants.

options.text: The quadratic algorithm will win at every future size
options.explanation: Its faster growth can eventually outweigh the smaller constants.

options.text: Discard the benchmark because only the asymptotic label matters
options.explanation: Representative measurements are needed for a finite deployment decision.

questions.workedExample: Separate current input bounds from eventual growth. A simple implementation may have less setup, allocation and per-step overhead. Keep the measured range explicit and re-evaluate if input sizes grow; no exact crossover follows from the two labels alone.

questions.prompt: An image filter takes time proportional to pixel count. Both the image width and height double, while per-pixel processing cost stays the same. How does the processing work change?

options.text: It quadruples
options.explanation: Correct. There are twice as many rows and twice as many pixels in each row.

options.text: It doubles, because the resolution doubled
options.explanation: Each *side* doubled, but the filter's cost is in pixels. Doubling both width and height multiplies the pixel count by 4.

options.text: Sixteen-fold: a square image makes the filter quadratic
options.explanation: This squares twice. The filter is linear in pixels, and pixels already grow with the square of the side. 2 times the side gives 4 times the pixels gives 4 times the time.

options.text: It stays the same, because the filter is linear
options.explanation: Linear means proportional to pixel count. The count has increased.

lessons.title: Proving an upper bound
lessons.summary: Use fixed constants to prove or disprove a Big-O claim.
lessons.body:
Big-O gives an eventual upper bound on growth. It does not promise an exact operation count, and it does not itself mean "worst case". First choose the cost function being discussed, such as worst-case comparisons over inputs of each size.

## One fixed multiplier must keep working

For a nonnegative cost, the definition is:

```formula essential
f(n) = O(g(n))
0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c g(n) for all n ≥ n_0
where
f(n): the nonnegative cost being bounded, in counted operations
g(n): the eventually positive comparison function, in the same cost model
n: the input size, a nonnegative integer
O: Big-O; the first line holds when fixed constants make the second line true
c: one positive multiplier independent of input size
n_0: a fixed starting input size beyond which the bound must always hold
≤, ≥: at most, at least
In words: beyond a fixed starting size, the cost never exceeds one fixed multiple of the comparison function.
```

The multiplier absorbs constant factors. The threshold allows a finite set of small inputs to behave differently. Neither may keep changing as the input grows.

For example, a scan with fixed setup work still has a linear upper bound. Choose a multiplier larger than its per-item cost; beyond some point, the spare allowance covers the setup on every later input. Matching only the per-item cost leaves no allowance for positive setup work.

A quadratic cost cannot have a linear upper bound. As inputs grow, work per item keeps increasing, so every proposed fixed linear multiplier is eventually exceeded.

## True can still be unhelpful

Binary search halves a sorted range and has a logarithmic worst-case comparison count, assuming constant-cost indexing and comparisons. It also has a linear upper bound, because linear growth eventually exceeds logarithmic growth. Both statements are true; the logarithmic bound is more informative.

Testing a few sizes cannot prove a bound for every later size. Use the mechanism or a mathematical argument. A ratio that grows without bound is one way to disprove an upper bound; oscillating ratios may require returning to the definition.

## Key takeaways
- Big-O permits one fixed multiplier and one fixed starting threshold.
- A valid bound must hold at every sufficiently large input size.
- Prefer a tight useful upper bound over a needlessly loose one.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

options.explanation: Correct. The extra allowance eventually covers fixed setup work on every later input.

options.text: Let the multiplier increase whenever a larger input breaks the bound
options.explanation: The Big-O multiplier must be fixed independently of input size.

options.text: Use a larger fixed multiplier to make the bound hold from an earlier threshold
options.explanation: Correct. A looser multiplier can absorb more setup work at small sizes.

options.explanation: A bound must hold for every sufficiently large input, not just tested examples.

options.text: Match per-item cost exactly and ignore positive setup work
options.explanation: That proposed upper expression leaves no allowance for the positive setup cost.

A larger multiplier can work earlier, but neither choice may keep changing with input size. Measurements can check examples, not prove the universal claim.

questions.prompt: In a code review, you write that a binary search over n items is `O(n)`. A colleague says that is wrong because binary search is `O(log n)`, where log denotes the base-two logarithm. Who is right? Assume a sorted random-access array and constant-cost comparisons.

options.text: Both statements are true, but O(log n) is the tighter and more useful one
options.explanation: Correct. A logarithmic bound also has a linear upper bound. The latter is true but loose; report the tightest useful bound. Here n is item count.

options.text: The colleague: an algorithm has exactly one Big-O
options.explanation: Big-O is an upper bound, and any function that grows at least as fast as the true cost is a valid upper bound. An algorithm belongs to many O classes.

options.text: You are: O(n) is safer because it covers the worst case
options.explanation: Binary search's worst case is still Θ(log n). O(n) is not 'safer', just less informative. Here n is the input item count.

options.text: Neither: binary search is Θ(1) in the best case, so its Big-O is O(1)
options.explanation: The best case (target found at the first midpoint) is Θ(1), but O bounds the cost from above over the inputs you are discussing. O(1) is not an upper bound on the worst case.

questions.workedExample: Binary search halves the remaining sorted range, so its worst-case comparison count is logarithmic in item count n. A linear function eventually exceeds a logarithm, making the linear upper bound true but loose. State the tighter logarithmic bound and the input case; Big-O alone does not select a case.

lessons.title: Lower and tight bounds
lessons.summary: Distinguish lower bounds, tight bounds and input cases.
lessons.body:
An upper bound says how fast a cost can grow. A lower bound says how slowly it cannot grow. A tight bound combines both for the same cost function.

## Lower and tight bounds

Big-Omega gives an eventual lower bound:

```formula essential
f(n) = Ω(g(n))
f(n) ≥ c g(n) for all n ≥ n_0
where
f(n): a nonnegative cost function
g(n): an eventually positive comparison function
n: input size
Ω: Big-Omega; the first line holds when fixed constants satisfy the second
c: a fixed positive lower-bound multiplier
n_0: a fixed starting size
≥: at least
In words: after a fixed starting size, the cost never falls below a fixed positive multiple of the comparison function.
```

Big-Theta puts the cost between two such bounds:

```formula essential
f(n) = Θ(g(n))
c_1 g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c_2 g(n)
for all n ≥ n_0
where
f(n): a nonnegative cost function
g(n): an eventually positive comparison function
n: input size
Θ: Big-Theta; the first line holds when the displayed bounds hold
c_1, c_2: fixed positive lower and upper multipliers
n_0: a fixed starting size
≤, ≥: at most, at least
In words: the cost stays between two fixed multiples of the same growth function, pinning down its growth up to constant factors.
```

## Bounds and input cases answer different questions

For insertion sort on n items, already sorted input takes Θ(n) time; reverse-sorted distinct input takes Θ(n²). Thus the worst-case function has a tight quadratic bound and the best-case function a tight linear bound. All inputs share a quadratic upper bound and a linear lower bound, but not one common tight bound depending only on item count.

O does not mean worst case, and Omega does not mean best case. State the input case separately.

Nor must a function fit a familiar growth class. Suppose its cost is one step at every odd size and one step per item at every even size. It has a linear upper bound and constant lower bound. The even sizes defeat a constant upper bound; the odd sizes defeat a linear lower bound. Its piecewise description is still an exact description.

## Key takeaways
- Theta needs matching upper and lower growth bounds.
- Specify best, average or worst case separately from the notation.
- Irregular costs need not match a familiar monotone growth class.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

questions.prompt: Insertion sort on n items takes `Θ(n)` time on already-sorted input and `Θ(n^2)` time on reverse-sorted input (Θ means "grows at exactly this rate, up to constants"). Which statement about its running time over **all** inputs of size n is correct?

options.explanation: Correct. Every input has a quadratic upper bound and a linear lower bound, but the input cases do not share one tight bound.

options.explanation: True. On even sizes the cost equals the input size; on odd sizes it is smaller. A linear upper bound covers both.
True. Every value is at least one, so the function has a constant lower bound.

lessons.title: Simplifying asymptotic expressions
lessons.summary: Drop dominated terms while preserving distinctions between exponential bases.
lessons.body:
Simplifying a cost means keeping the part that determines eventual growth. Here n is input size; log denotes a logarithm with a fixed base greater than one.

## Remove details only when the bound permits it

- Fixed positive multipliers do not change a tight growth class.
- In a finite sum of nonnegative familiar growth functions, keep the fastest-growing term. For example, cubic work eventually dominates quadratic-times-log work and fixed overhead.
- Two sequential phases add their costs. Independent nested phases multiply their counts.
- Independent input dimensions must remain separate unless their relationship is known.

The rule is about growth, not exact equality. Two functions can share a quadratic upper bound while having quite different values, or even different tight growth rates. A linear function and a quadratic function both have a quadratic upper bound.

## Logarithm bases and exponential bases behave differently

Changing between two fixed logarithm bases multiplies the value by a constant. It changes an exact count, but not the logarithmic growth class. The useful conversion is available as reference:

```formula reference
log_a(n) = log_b(n) / log_b(a)
where
log_a, log_b: logarithms to bases a and b
a, b: fixed bases greater than one
n: positive input size
In words: changing between two fixed logarithm bases rescales the value by a fixed multiplier, so the growth class stays the same.
```

Changing an exponential base is different. Choosing among three possibilities per item creates more candidates than choosing among two. Their ratio itself grows exponentially, so a constant multiplier cannot absorb that difference.

A fixed power of a logarithm eventually grows more slowly than any positive power of input size. A fixed polynomial eventually grows more slowly than an exponential with fixed base greater than one. "Eventually" matters: a very large polynomial exponent or coefficient can delay that order far beyond practical inputs.

## Key takeaways
- Drop coefficients and dominated terms when describing eventual growth.
- A shared upper bound is not a statement of equal cost.
- Fixed log bases change constants; exponential bases can change growth classes.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

lessons.title: Ordering growth with limits
lessons.summary: Use ratios and the growth ladder to compare unfamiliar cost functions.
lessons.body:
Compare growth by asking whether the gap between two costs keeps widening. Here n is input size; logarithms have a fixed base greater than one.

## Ratios give a useful test

Divide the first eventually positive function by the second and consider increasingly large inputs:

| Ratio approaches | What it establishes |
|---|---|
| Zero | the first grows strictly more slowly |
| A fixed positive number | the same tight growth rate |
| Infinity | the first grows strictly faster |

A ratio approaching zero is called **little-o**. These are sufficient conclusions when the limit exists. A tight bound does not require convergence: a ratio can keep oscillating between two positive constants. If there is no limit, inspect bounds directly.

## A growth ladder

| Slower to faster | Example mechanism |
|---|---|
| Constant | index a fixed-size array slot |
| Logarithmic | repeatedly halve a search range |
| Square root | count up to the square root of a numeric bound |
| Linear | scan every item |
| Linear times log | merge over logarithmically many levels |
| Quadratic, then cubic | all pairs, then all triples |
| Fixed-base exponential | enumerate subsets |
| Factorial | enumerate all orderings |

This compares eventual growth with the same input measure. A square-root divisor search measured in numeric value is still exponential when measured in bit length.

Factorial counts multiply the positive integers up to the item count. Taking a logarithm turns that product into a sum of logarithms. There are at most n terms each no larger than the logarithm of n, and a constant fraction are within a constant of that largest logarithm. Thus the logarithm of the factorial has Θ(n log n) growth. This underlies the worst-case comparison-sorting lower bound.

A **quasi-polynomial** example raises input size to its logarithm. It eventually outgrows every fixed polynomial yet remains below a fixed-base exponential. Comparing both expressions as powers of the same base reveals the order; a single measured size cannot prove it.

## Key takeaways
- Ratio limits reveal relative growth when the limit exists.
- A finite-range measurement is not a proof of eventual order.
- Factorial growth is enormous, but its logarithm is linear times log.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

lessons.title: Counting sequential and nested loops
lessons.summary: Add sequential work and count the true length of dependent inner loops.
lessons.body:
Count how many times the meaningful operation runs, not how many loops are visible. Here n and m are independent input sizes. Assume each counted operation has constant cost.

## Add sequential work; multiply independent nested work

A list scan followed by a square-grid scan adds the two workloads. If n is list length and m is the grid's side length, the result is O(n + m²). Without a relationship between the list and grid sizes, neither contribution can be discarded.

A loop that restarts a full inner loop on every pass multiplies the two counts. A fixed inner bound, such as a hundred checks, changes the coefficient but leaves a full outer scan linear.

## Dependent bounds need a sum

```python
# n is the nonnegative input bound.
for i in range(n):
    # Earlier positions only.
    for j in range(i):
        work()
```

Here `work()` stands for one constant-cost operation. The inner lengths grow from zero to one less than the outer bound. Their total is roughly half a full square, so the work is Θ(n²). Halving a quadratic amount does not make it linear.

For a direct growth argument, the final half of outer passes each do at least about half the maximum inner work. That already gives a quadratic lower bound; the full square supplies a quadratic upper bound. No exact sum is needed.

Three ordered distinct positions similarly occupy a fixed fraction of a full cube, giving cubic growth. But nesting alone proves nothing: different dependent ranges can produce linear or logarithmic totals.

## Include hidden work

A function call costs its body, not one step. `sorted()` does comparisons and moves elements. Printing can format values and wait for output. State explicitly when counting calls instead of their elapsed costs. For a worst-case branch, analyse the most expensive path that a valid input can actually reach.

## Key takeaways
- Sequential phases add; independently repeated phases multiply.
- Sum actual inner lengths when bounds depend on the outer position.
- Count the work inside calls and state the cost model.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

lessons.title: Doubling and growing inner loops
lessons.summary: Recognise logarithmic loops and sum a geometric series of inner-loop lengths.
lessons.body:
Repeated multiplication reaches a large bound much sooner than repeated addition. Throughout, n is a positive integer input bound and `work()` is one constant-cost step.

## Count doublings, not the final value

```python
i = 1
while i < n:
    i *= 2
```

The values before each update are one, two, four, eight and so on. A bound of sixteen needs four updates; seventeen needs one more. Doubling the bound adds only about one pass, giving logarithmic work. A fixed multiplier greater than one gives the same growth class. Integer division by a fixed factor has a similar effect when its stopping condition guarantees termination.

A loop that increments by one while `i * i <= n` instead makes about the square root of the bound in updates. Inspect the update and stopping rule together.

## Restarting changes the total

Restart a full doubling loop for each of n outer iterations and the total is Θ(n log n). But this different pattern is linear:

```python
i = 1
while i < n:
    for j in range(i):
        work()
    i *= 2
```

The inner lengths double. All earlier lengths together are smaller than twice the last length, and the last length is a substantial fraction of the bound. This **geometric series** therefore gives Θ(n) total work. Charging the largest inner loop on every pass overestimates it.

Another trap starts the inner doubling variable at the outer value:

```python
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    j = i
    while j < n:
        j *= 2
```

Most starting values need very few doublings. Almost all permit a first update, about half a second, about a quarter a third. These shrinking groups sum to linear work; the outer scan is also linear. It is Θ(n), not linear times log.

## Key takeaways
- Multiplicative updates often give logarithmic iteration counts.
- Sum the inner loops actually performed, including their starting values.
- Geometrically changing lengths can give a linear total.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

lessons.title: Loops with a variable step
lessons.summary: Sum the shrinking inner counts in a harmonic loop.
lessons.body:
An inner loop can become shorter even when its endpoint stays fixed. Here n is a positive input bound and `work()` is one constant-cost step.

## Watch the step size

```python
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    # Start at zero; exclude n.
    for j in range(0, n, i):
        work()
```

With step one, the inner loop visits every position. With step two it visits about half; step three about a third. Each length is the bound divided by the step, rounded up. The total does not equal the largest inner length multiplied by the outer count.

These contributions form a **harmonic sum**, whose growth is logarithmic. Multiplying by the original bound gives Θ(n log n) work. Rounding adds less than one extra step per outer pass, so it cannot change that class.

## Why a logarithmic factor appears

Group step sizes into bands that double: one, then two to three, then four to seven, and so on. A later band has about twice as many step sizes, but each inner loop is about half as long. Each complete band therefore contributes work proportional to the original bound. There are logarithmically many bands.

This differs from a geometric sum of inner lengths. In a geometric sum, doubling the index halves the entire next contribution. Here there are many step sizes between successive powers of two, and their combined contributions matter.

| Inner-loop pattern | Total growth |
|---|---|
| Same full range each time | quadratic |
| Length grows with outer position | quadratic |
| Doubling outer value sets inner length | linear |
| Outer value sets the inner step | linear times log |

The shared lesson is to read the actual range. Similar-looking nested loops need not have similar cost.

## Key takeaways
- A larger step means fewer inner iterations.
- Harmonic contributions accumulate across logarithmically many bands.
- Integer rounding does not change this loop's tight growth bound.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

lessons.title: Recursive work and hidden costs
lessons.summary: Count recursive calls and uncover work hidden inside ordinary Python operations.
lessons.body:
A short function can perform a large amount of work. Count all recursive calls and the work each call performs outside its children. Here n is the recursive argument or list length, as stated.

## Repeated subproblems multiply work

```python
# fib(5) returns 5.
def fib(n):
    if n < 2:
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
```

Both children repeat calculations already performed elsewhere. Drawing the calls for `fib(5)` reveals repeated `fib(3)` and `fib(2)` work. The total call count grows exponentially. More precisely it is Θ(φⁿ), where n is the nonnegative argument and φ is the golden ratio, about 1.618. The branches have different depths, so a full binary tree with base two is a loose upper bound, not the tight call count.

Memoisation stores completed answers by argument. Only a linear number of distinct arguments need calculating. This gives a linear number of additions; it does not make arithmetic on increasingly large Python integers constant-time.

## A line of Python is not one operation

For CPython lists, indexing and reading length are constant-cost in the usual model. Membership scans may inspect every item. Front removal shifts remaining references. Slicing creates a new list of references. Appending is constant amortised time, allowing occasional resizing.

```python
# unique([3, 1, 3]) returns [3, 1].
def unique(items):
    seen = []
    out = []
    for x in items:
        if x not in seen:
            seen.append(x)
            out.append(x)
    return out
```

All-distinct input makes each membership scan longer, giving quadratic comparisons. Replacing `seen` with a set and using `add` gives expected linear work for hashable values with constant-cost hashing and equality under a suitable hashing model. Keeping `out` as a list preserves first-occurrence order.

A recursive binary search that slices its chosen half also hides work. Its comparison count is logarithmic, but the copied halves form a linear total in the original list length. Passing index bounds avoids those copies.

## Key takeaways
- Count the whole call tree, including repeated subproblems.
- Include comparison, hashing, copying and shifting costs.
- Changing the representation can remove repeated work while preserving the result.

## Further reading
- [CPython 3.14 list implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/3.14/Objects/listobject.c)
- [Python caching tools](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/functools.html)

lessons.title: Best, average and worst cases
lessons.summary: State which inputs or random choices a performance claim describes.
lessons.body:
Inputs of the same size can follow different paths. Here n is the number of items and equality comparisons have constant cost.

```python
def find(xs, target):
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        if x == target:
            return i
    return -1  # Target is absent.
```

## State what is being averaged

The best case finds the target first: constant work. The worst case finds it last or fails to find it: linear work. If a present target is equally likely to occupy any position, the average search examines about half the list and is still linear.

That average depends on its assumptions. A workload that frequently requests the first item differs from one with mostly absent targets. "Average" without an input distribution is incomplete.

For a randomised algorithm, expected time can instead average over the algorithm's random choices while holding the input fixed. Quicksort with distinct keys and fresh uniformly random pivots has expected Θ(n log n) time on every fixed input of n items. A first-element pivot on sorted distinct input instead gives quadratic work. An adversary adapting to predictable random choices falls outside the fixed-input model.

## Early exits need a remaining worst case

An early return can improve some inputs dramatically. It changes worst-case growth only if every valid input avoids the previous worst path. To assess a claim, try to construct an input that still forces the full scan or unbalanced recursion.

Worst-case guarantees are useful for hostile inputs and deadlines. Average or expected bounds can also be useful, provided their assumptions fit the application. A fast best case alone gives little assurance about an actual workload.

## Key takeaways
- Best and worst case select extreme inputs of a given size.
- Average case requires an input distribution.
- Expected time can average random choices for each fixed input.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

lessons.title: Counting auxiliary memory
lessons.summary: Distinguish extra storage, output memory and lazy value generation.
lessons.body:
Space complexity measures the largest amount of memory needed at once. It does not count every object ever created if earlier objects have already been released.

## Say what the count includes

**Total space** includes the stored input. **Auxiliary space** measures additional storage. State whether output is included: a function producing a new list has to store that result even if its working variables are few. Streaming input need not remain resident, so reading many items alone does not imply storing them all.

Here n is input length or table side length. The following counts treat each value and reference as one memory word and include returned collections:

```python
def total(xs):
    s = 0
    for x in xs:
        s += x
    return s

def reversed_copy(xs):
    return xs[::-1]

def table(n):
    return [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
```

The sum retains a constant number of values. The reverse creates n reference slots. The square table retains n rows each containing n slots, giving quadratic space. A triangle of increasingly long rows still contains a quadratic number of slots, even when every slot refers to the same zero object.

## Produce values when needed

```python
# Both produce 30 when n is 5.
sum([x * x for x in range(n)])
sum(x * x for x in range(n))
```

The first expression builds all squares before summing. The second is a generator expression: `sum` requests one square at a time. Under the atomic-value model, this removes the linear intermediate collection and uses constant auxiliary storage. It still computes every square.

Python integers can grow in bit length. A constant number of integer objects therefore does not necessarily mean constant bytes. Also, a generator can retain a large source or other state; its memory saving depends on the particular producer and consumer.

## Key takeaways
- Measure peak live storage and state input/output conventions.
- Shared values still require slots in a collection.
- Streaming avoids storing all intermediate values when the consumer can process them one at a time.

## Further reading
- [Python sequence types and integers](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/stdtypes.html)

lessons.title: Pending calls and recursion depth
lessons.summary: Count live stack frames and understand why caching does not remove the first recursive descent.
lessons.body:
Every call that is waiting for a child needs a frame containing its local state. Space follows the deepest chain of pending calls, together with data those calls retain.

```python
def fact(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    return n * fact(n - 1)
```

For a positive argument n, this creates a chain down to one. Under a model treating each number as atomic and each frame as fixed-size, stack space is Θ(n). An iterative version holds a constant number of values. Actual Python integers grow: the factorial result alone needs Θ(n log n) bits for sufficiently large n.

## Calls over time are not simultaneous frames

Naive Fibonacci makes exponentially many calls but follows one child at a time. Completed branches release their frames before later siblings finish. Its maximum depth is linear in the argument, so its stack is linear in the atomic-value model.

Recursive binary search with index bounds has logarithmic depth because it halves the range. Merge sort also has logarithmic depth, but its merge buffer requires linear extra space. Count retained buffers as well as frames.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A stack of unfinished tasks
> When a task depends on a smaller task, put a reminder aside until that task finishes.
>
> **How it maps:** Each reminder is a pending frame. The tallest pile matters for space, even if many reminders are used throughout the day.
>
> **Where it stops:** Frames can retain differently sized objects; counting reminders alone assumes fixed-size state.

## Caching does not shorten the first descent

Memoisation avoids repeating completed calculations. With an empty cache, a Fibonacci-style function still descends through consecutive smaller arguments before any result is available. It can hit the configured recursion limit despite doing only linearly many distinct computations.

Use `sys.getrecursionlimit()` to inspect that limit. Raising it is not a substitute for a space analysis and can be unsafe for some interpreter and C-extension call paths. Python does not eliminate recursive Python tail calls. A bottom-up loop avoids the recursive chain; retaining only the previous two values also avoids a full answer cache. Their growing bit lengths remain a separate cost.

## Key takeaways
- Count simultaneously live frames and retained data.
- Exponential call counts can coexist with linear stack depth.
- A bottom-up loop can remove a cold recursive descent that caching preserves.

## Further reading
- [Python recursion limits](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/sys.html)
- [Python caching tools](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/functools.html)

lessons.title: In-place transformations
lessons.summary: Mutate an existing list and bound quicksort stack depth by recursing on the smaller side.
lessons.body:
An in-place transformation reuses the input storage. Under the strict convention it uses only constant auxiliary space; some descriptions allow a logarithmic recursion stack. State which convention you mean.

```python
def reverse_in_place(xs):
    i, j = 0, len(xs) - 1
    while i < j:
        xs[i], xs[j] = xs[j], xs[i]
        i += 1
        j -= 1
```

This keeps two positions and swaps within the existing list. It returns `None`. In contrast, `xs[::-1]` allocates a new list. Here n is the list length; the first uses O(1) auxiliary words and the copy uses O(n).

## Mutation has a cost beyond memory

Other references to the same list observe the changes. If the caller needs the original order, copying first removes the storage saving. An in-place algorithm can also be harder to implement correctly. Choose it because its trade-offs fit the caller, not merely because its space label is smaller.

Mutating an input is not proof of constant auxiliary space. CPython's `list.sort()` mutates the list but may allocate a merge buffer proportional to its length. Heapsort can sort an array using constant auxiliary words.

## Bound quicksort's stack separately from its time

Ordinary quicksort that recurses on both partitions can build a linear-depth chain with repeatedly unbalanced pivots. Recurse only on the smaller partition and process the larger partition with a loop. Every additional recursive frame then receives at most half its parent's items, bounding stack depth by O(log n).

Changing the order of two recursive calls is insufficient: the larger side must become a loop. This change fixes stack growth even with a poor pivot rule, but it does not remove quadratic worst-case comparisons. Random pivots improve expected time under the stated randomness model; a fallback such as heapsort can provide a worst-case time bound.

## Key takeaways
- Distinguish mutation from constant auxiliary storage.
- Check whether other code still needs the original input.
- Recursing on the smaller side bounds stack depth without necessarily fixing runtime.

## Further reading
- [CPython 3.14 sorting design](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/3.14/Objects/listsort.txt)
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

lessons.title: Memory trade-offs and real storage
lessons.summary: Choose a representation and balance extra memory against speed.
lessons.body:
A faster algorithm may need more storage. A smaller representation may let the same algorithm handle a much larger input. Here n is the number of input items.

## Spend memory where it removes repeated work

Checking duplicates with a hash set uses expected linear time and linear extra storage under suitable hashing assumptions. Sorting in place and comparing neighbours trades more computation for less extra storage, but changes input order. A strict constant-space claim needs a suitable sort, such as heapsort.

For a pair-sum problem on a reorderable array, sorting followed by two positions moving inward avoids keeping a hash set. When the current sum is too small, advance the lower end; when too large, retreat the upper end. The ordering makes those decisions safe.

**Precomputation** is another trade-off. Prefix sums store the total before each position. A range total is then the prefix at the end minus the prefix at the start. Building the prefixes costs linear work and storage, while each query uses one subtraction for fixed-size values. Updates can invalidate later prefixes, so the benefit depends on the workload.

## A growth class is not a byte budget

A Python list stores references to objects. A packed numeric array stores fixed-width values directly. Both have linear storage growth, but their per-item sizes differ.

For a hypothetical representation with eight-byte entries, ten million entries need an 80 MB data buffer, using decimal megabytes. A list of separately allocated Python integers also needs object headers, references and possible spare capacity. `sys.getsizeof` reports the immediate object size, not recursively all objects it references.

Use the actual build and value range when budgeting. The standard `array` module exposes `itemsize`; its type widths depend on the C implementation. A signed 64-bit representation cannot hold arbitrary-size Python integers. Leave room for runtime state and temporary buffers during construction or conversion.

## Key takeaways
- Compare time, extra storage and permission to mutate together.
- Precomputed answers help repeated queries but introduce storage and update costs.
- Measure representation overhead and peak construction memory, not just asymptotic space.

## Further reading
- [Python packed arrays](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/array.html)
- [Python object-size measurement](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/sys.html)

lessons.title: Dynamic arrays and total append cost
lessons.summary: Bound the total writes and copies over a sequence of dynamic-array appends.
lessons.body:
A dynamic array stores items in a contiguous region with spare capacity. Most appends fill a spare slot. When it is full, a resize may allocate a larger region and copy existing items.

## Analyse a sequence, not just its slowest operation

Consider an idealised array that starts empty with capacity one and doubles when full. Count one unit per copied or newly written element; ignore allocator details. Here n is the number of appends.

A resize-triggering append can copy every current item, so one operation can be linear in the current length. But it is too pessimistic to charge that cost to every append. After doubling, many spare slots can be filled before the next copy.

The copied capacities are one, two, four, eight and so on. This geometric series is bounded by a constant multiple of its largest term. Adding the one write per append therefore gives linear total work. For this model, total work is below three units per append when spread across the sequence.

**Aggregate analysis** establishes a bound for the whole sequence, then divides by its length. Constant amortised append cost means any sequence of n appends from the stated starting state costs O(n) total work. It does not mean every append is fast.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Moving to a bigger bookshelf
> Moving books to a shelf with twice the space is expensive, but many later books fit without another move.
>
> **How it maps:** Spare shelf space corresponds to spare capacity; increasingly separated moves explain the linear total copying.
>
> **Where it stops:** The proof counts item moves under a fixed growth policy. Real allocation and item-copy costs may differ.

## No probability is involved

Amortised analysis averages cost across an operation sequence, not across random inputs. The sequence bound is deterministic under its model. Starting with a large full array would require accounting for that initial state; the from-empty proof cannot silently charge its first resize to earlier appends that never occurred.

CPython lists grow with spare capacity rather than precisely doubling. The same geometric-growth idea explains their amortised append behaviour; exact capacity sequences are implementation details.

## Key takeaways
- Rare expensive appends can coexist with linear total sequence cost.
- Amortised guarantees need a starting state and operation policy.
- Amortisation is different from average-case probability.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Amortized Analysis](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/09-amortize.pdf)
- [CPython 3.14 list implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/3.14/Objects/listobject.c)

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes what 'append is O(1) **amortised**' means? Assume the array starts empty.

options.text: Each append is O(1) on average, assuming the list sizes are random
options.explanation: This describes average-case analysis, which needs a probability distribution. Amortised analysis uses no probability.

options.text: Every individual append takes O(1) time
options.explanation: Not true: the append that triggers a resize copies every element, which is Θ(n), proportional to the n elements already stored. Amortised bounds allow occasional expensive operations. Here n is the append count.

options.text: Append is O(1) except in the worst case, where it is O(n)
options.explanation: This mixes up single-operation worst case with sequence cost. The amortised bound *is* a worst-case bound, over sequences.

options.text: Any sequence of n appends takes O(n) total time, so the cost per append averages to O(1) over the sequence
options.explanation: Correct. Amortised cost is a guarantee about the total for any sequence, even a worst-case one, divided by the number of operations.

Their total copying and writing is linear in append count n. Sharing that total across the sequence gives a constant amortised cost without making assumptions about random inputs.

options.text: A resize never copies existing items

options.text: Copying memory costs one operation regardless of length

options.text: Only random append sequences get expensive resizes

questions.prompt: Why do n single-item append calls to an initially empty CPython list have linear total work under the usual constant-cost reference model?

options.text: Because the list over-allocates by a constant factor, so the copying costs form a geometric series that sums to O(n)
options.explanation: Correct. Proportional spare capacity spaces copying events apart, giving linear total copying. Exact allocation sizes are implementation details.

options.text: Because Python lists are linked lists, so appending never copies
options.explanation: CPython lists are arrays of pointers, not linked lists. They do copy (or reallocate) when they run out of room.

lessons.title: Banking credits for expensive steps
lessons.summary: Use the accounting method to save credit during cheap operations.
lessons.body:
The accounting method explains an amortised bound by saving credit during cheap operations and spending it during expensive ones. Credit is a proof device, measured in counted work units; no actual runtime balance is needed.

## Charge enough to fund later copies

Use the doubling-array model, starting empty with capacity one. Count each copy and new-element write as one unit. Charge three units per append: one pays for the immediate write and two are saved.

Before a resize, saved credit pays to copy all existing elements. After doubling, the appends that fill the new half save enough to pay for the next whole-array copy. The first append also creates enough credit for the first small resize. Inductively, the bank never needs to go below zero.

Why save for older elements too? At the last resize those elements spent their previous copying credit. New appends must rebuild credit for the whole array, not just themselves. Banking two units per new element covers both halves by the next full state.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Saving for an annual bill
> Regular payments can put aside money for an occasional larger bill.
>
> **How it maps:** Cheap appends contribute spare credit; resizing consumes that saved credit. A nonnegative balance proves earlier charges cover the real cost.
>
> **Where it stops:** There is no interest, prediction or random arrival rate. The algorithm proof must cover every allowed sequence from its stated initial state.

## The balance is the proof obligation

If a proposed charge lets the bank become negative, that accounting argument has failed: it is spending work credits never collected. This does not automatically prove the algorithm is slow; it means the proposed charges or invariant are insufficient.

Starting from a pre-populated array requires an initial-credit allowance. Supporting deletion requires a separate argument for the shrinking policy. A proof for append-only sequences does not automatically cover arbitrary updates.

## Key takeaways
- Cheap operations can prepay future expensive work.
- Credits must cover every allowed prefix of the sequence.
- A negative balance invalidates the proposed accounting proof.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Amortized Analysis](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/09-amortize.pdf)

options.text: Previously collected credit plus the current charge must cover actual work
options.explanation: Correct. The proof must never spend more than it has charged.

options.text: Every item can be charged only when it is copied
options.explanation: The method deliberately charges earlier cheap operations for future work.

options.text: The resize must happen at a randomly chosen time
options.explanation: The proof concerns all allowed sequences and needs no randomness.

If the balance becomes negative, the proposed charges or invariant have failed; expecting later operations does not repair a bound for a sequence that ends now.

lessons.title: Potential as stored work
lessons.summary: Use changes in a potential function to prove an amortised bound.
lessons.body:
A potential function tracks saved work for an entire data structure. It should rise during cheap operations and fall when expensive work consumes that saving.

## Actual cost plus the change in stored work

```formula essential
a_i = c_i + Φ_i − Φ_{i−1}
where
a_i: the amortised cost charged for operation i, in work units
c_i: its actual cost in the same work units
Φ_i: potential after operation i, in work units
Φ_{i−1}: potential before that operation
i: the operation number, starting at one
Φ: capital phi, the chosen potential function of the structure's state
In words: charge the actual work plus any newly stored potential; releasing potential reduces the charge for an expensive operation.
```

When these charges are added, every intermediate potential appears once positively and once negatively. Those terms cancel, leaving actual total work plus final potential minus starting potential. Starting at zero and keeping potential nonnegative therefore makes the amortised total an upper bound on actual total work for every sequence prefix. More generally, final potential must not fall below the starting value for that same bound without an extra initial allowance.

## A doubling-array example

Count copies and writes as one work unit each. Start with an empty capacity-zero array, allocate one slot on its first append, then double when full. For this append-only policy the array is at least half full after its first append. One useful reference choice is:

```formula reference
Φ = 2s − K
where
Φ: stored potential, in work units
s: the number of stored elements
K: capacity in element slots
In words: potential increases as the array fills and drops when doubling creates spare room, releasing credit to offset copying.
```

A cheap append stores two potential units alongside its one write. A resize costs many copies, but the drop in potential offsets them. The resulting charge is at most three units per append, including the initial append. This is a proof about counted work, not a claim that each append takes the same time.

Choosing potential is part of designing the proof. The element count alone need not be suitable, and this append-only potential is not automatically valid after arbitrary deletions.

## Key takeaways
- Potential change connects cheap and expensive operations.
- Intermediate potential values cancel in a sequence total.
- Check the starting state and nonnegative-balance condition.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Amortized Analysis](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/09-amortize.pdf)

options.text: If Φ starts at 0 and never becomes negative, the sum of amortised costs bounds the sum of actual costs

lessons.title: Growth policies and safe shrinking
lessons.summary: Choose growth and shrink thresholds that avoid repeated full-array copying.
lessons.body:
Amortised append performance depends on the growth rule. Assume a resize copies all current items, each copy costs one unit, and the array starts empty with fixed initial capacity.

## Fixed increments keep resizes too frequent

Adding a hundred slots at a time eventually means copying a huge array after only another hundred appends. Copy sizes grow in an arithmetic progression. Across n appends the total copying is quadratic in n, so amortised cost per append grows linearly.

Multiplying capacity by a fixed factor greater than one instead creates room for proportionally more appends each time. Copy sizes form a geometric progression and total copying is linear. Doubling, growing by one half, and growing by a fixed one eighth all give constant amortised append cost with suitable integer rounding.

A smaller fixed factor saves spare capacity but causes more copying. Exact growth factors are implementation details; CPython 3.14 uses proportional over-allocation with rounding and small-size adjustments. A bulk insertion can follow additional rules, so do not infer its allocation from a single-item append example.

## Separate growth and shrink thresholds

Suppose the array doubles when full and halves as soon as it becomes half full. Append to a full array, then pop: the append grows it, the pop shrinks it, and the next append must grow it again. Every operation can copy nearly the whole array.

Use **hysteresis**: for example, grow when full but shrink only at a quarter full, halving capacity. After shrinking, the array is half full; after growth it is roughly half full. A substantial number of updates must occur before another resize. With a fixed minimum capacity, this supports constant amortised push and pop cost.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A thermostat's dead band
> Heating does not switch on and off at exactly the same temperature boundary.
>
> **How it maps:** Separated thresholds prevent tiny reversals from repeatedly triggering an expensive state change.
>
> **Where it stops:** Array guarantees follow counted updates and copying costs, not physical heating dynamics.

## Key takeaways
- Fixed-factor growth spaces expensive copies apart.
- Fixed-increment growth leads to quadratic total copying.
- Separate growth and shrink thresholds prevent repeated resizing at one boundary.

## Further reading
- [CPython 3.14 list implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/3.14/Objects/listobject.c)
- [Erickson: Amortized Analysis](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/09-amortize.pdf)

lessons.title: Amortisation beyond arrays and latency
lessons.summary: Apply sequence reasoning to counters and queues while recognising latency spikes.
lessons.body:
A good sequence bound does not guarantee a short delay for each operation. Here n counts operations or stored items, as each example states.

## Follow each piece of work across its lifetime

A binary counter starting at zero flips its lowest bit on every increment, the next about half as often and later bits progressively less often. Across n increments, the total number of flips is linear in n even though a single carry can flip many bits.

A queue can use an `inbox` stack and an `outbox` stack. Enqueue pushes to the inbox. Dequeue pops the outbox; only when it is empty does it transfer the inbox by repeated pop-and-push operations. The reversal restores first-in-first-out order.

Each item enters the inbox once, transfers at most once and leaves the outbox once. Starting empty, total stack operations are proportional to total queue operations, assuming each stack operation is constant cost. One dequeue can still pay for a large transfer.

## Throughput and deadlines are different requirements

A dynamic-array append may relocate all existing elements. An amortised constant bound permits that delay. A system with a strict per-operation deadline must inspect allocation, relocation and other slow paths rather than relying on the average sequence charge.

Possible approaches include reserving enough capacity before the hot path, filling a pre-sized container by index, using fixed-size chunks, or spreading migration work across updates. Each has costs: extra memory, more complicated lookup rules or allocation at chunk boundaries. None alone promises a fixed wall-clock deadline.

In Python, `[None] * n` creates a list with n actual elements. Fill those slots by index; appending instead adds after them. It is not an empty list with reserved capacity.

The proof also assumes updates progress through states. Reusing an old version of a persistent data structure can repeat expensive work without rebuilding credit. Such structures need an analysis of sharing and deferred work, not an automatic reuse of an imperative proof.

## Key takeaways
- Count how often each item or bit can incur work over a sequence.
- Amortised cost bounds total work, not tail latency.
- Preallocation or incremental work needs its own capacity and latency assumptions.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Amortized Analysis](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/09-amortize.pdf)
- [Python sequence operations](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/stdtypes.html)

options.text: Every increment flips exactly one bit
options.explanation: Carries can flip several trailing ones and a following zero.

options.text: The counter is assumed to receive random increments
options.explanation: The sequence proof is deterministic.

options.text: A bit can never flip again after it first becomes one
options.explanation: Bits repeatedly alternate; their different frequencies make the total small.

Their sum is bounded by a constant multiple of the increment count, starting from zero. This permits an occasional long carry while retaining constant amortised cost.

options.text: Every dequeue performs only one stack operation
options.explanation: A dequeue may first transfer a large inbox.

options.text: Every element is transferred again on every dequeue
options.explanation: Once in outbox, an element waits there until removed.

options.text: Each element performs only a fixed number of stack operations during its lifetime
options.explanation: Correct. It enters inbox, transfers once and leaves outbox once.

options.text: Both stacks stay constant-size
options.explanation: They can grow with queue length; the claim is about work per sequence, not constant storage.

questions.prompt: A low-latency trading service appends market events to a C++ `std::vector`. Mean latency is excellent, but the p99.99 latency shows rare multi-millisecond spikes that line up with the vector growing past a few hundred MB. What is the most appropriate fix?

options.text: Nothing: append is O(1) amortised, so the spikes must come from somewhere else
options.explanation: Amortised cost permits expensive individual relocations. The scenario’s measured correlation identifies a plausible slow path.

options.text: Reserve capacity up front (or use a chunked structure that never moves existing elements)
options.explanation: Correct. Reserving enough before the hot path prevents capacity-driven reallocation while that limit is respected. A chunked design can avoid moving prior elements, though new allocations and other costs still need measurement.

options.text: Switch to growing by a fixed 1 MB each time, so each resize is smaller
options.explanation: Each resize would still copy the whole vector (the copy is of existing data, not the new space), and resizes would become far more frequent. Total cost becomes quadratic.

options.text: Use a growth factor of 4 instead of 2
options.explanation: A larger factor reduces resize frequency but retains occasional full relocation and increases spare capacity. It does not guarantee a latency bound.

Reserve sufficient capacity before the hot path and enforce that bound, or choose a suitable chunked representation. Fixed-increment growth increases copying frequency; a larger factor still permits large relocations. Allocation and other runtime effects must also be measured before claiming a deadline guarantee.

lessons.title: Writing recurrences from code
lessons.summary: Separate recursive subproblem costs from each call’s own work.
lessons.body:
A recurrence describes a recursive call's cost using the costs of its children. Read three things from the code: how many calls it makes, how large their inputs are, and what work remains outside those calls.

## Read the control flow

```python
# a is sorted; lo and hi are inclusive.
def bsearch(a, t, lo, hi):
    if lo > hi:
        return -1
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] == t:
        return mid
    if a[mid] < t:
        return bsearch(a, t, mid + 1, hi)
    return bsearch(a, t, lo, mid - 1)
```

Only one branch executes. The function searches one roughly half-size range and does constant outside work, assuming constant-cost indexing, comparisons and index arithmetic. It passes bounds instead of copying a slice.

Merge sort instead solves both halves and merges their results. The merge visits the items in the current range. These different behaviours produce different recurrences:

```formula essential
T_search(n) = T_search(n/2) + Θ(1)
T_merge(n) = 2T_merge(n/2) + Θ(n)
where
T_search(n): binary search's worst-case counted work on n items
T_merge(n): merge sort's counted work on n items
n: the current range length
Θ: a tight growth bound, up to fixed positive multipliers
In words: binary search follows one half with constant outside work; merge sort follows both halves and also processes the whole current range.
```

These are asymptotic models with a fixed positive base-case cost. Half sizes are rounded as the actual ranges require; rounding does not change the stated growth for these algorithms. Binary search is logarithmic, while merge sort is linear times log in the original item count.

Do not count child work twice: the cost assigned to a child already contains everything it does. Conversely, do not forget copying, scanning or combining work in the parent. A function with two calls followed by a full scan has the same cost shape as merge sort even if its purpose is different.

## Key takeaways
- Count executed children, their sizes and outside work separately.
- Include a stopping rule and base-case cost.
- Similar recursion shapes can describe different algorithms.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

questions.prompt:
Which recurrence describes the running time of this function? T(n) is its running time when the range `lo` to `hi` holds n elements. Assume constant-cost indexing and arithmetic updates.

```python
# hi is excluded from this range.
def f(a, lo, hi):
    if hi - lo <= 1:
        return
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    # Recurse on both halves first.
    f(a, lo, mid)
    f(a, mid, hi)
    # Visit the entire current range.
    for i in range(lo, hi):
        a[i] += 1
```

options.explanation: This counts only one recursive call. The function recurses on both halves.

options.text: Two half-size calls plus constant work
options.explanation: This misses the loop, which does work proportional to the current range size, n, not constant.

options.text: Two half-size calls plus linear work
options.explanation:
Correct. Two recursive calls on halves, plus a linear loop over the current range. This is merge sort's recurrence, and solves to Θ(n log n), growing like n times the base-2 logarithm of n.

Here n is the current subproblem size.

options.text: Two calls one item smaller, plus linear work
options.explanation: The subproblems are halves (lo to mid, mid to hi), not one element smaller.

questions.workedExample: There are two executed recursive calls, each on roughly half the range. The loop then visits every position in the current range. Thus the recurrence has two half-size children plus linear outside work. With bounded positive base cases and constant-cost updates, that gives Θ(n log n) for range length n.

lessons.title: Adding up recursion trees
lessons.summary: Sum level costs to identify whether roots, levels or leaves dominate.
lessons.body:
A recursion tree turns recursive work into levels you can add. Each node is one call, labelled with only that call's outside work. Here n is the original input size; leaves have bounded positive cost.

## Three shapes explain many bounds

For two half-size children with linear outside work, each level processes the original input amount in total. More nodes are offset by smaller ranges. Halving produces logarithmically many levels, so total work is Θ(n log n).

```diagram
          whole
         /     \
       half    half
      /   \    /   \
   quarter quarter quarter quarter
```

This picture describes equal halves, not all possible recursion trees. For powers of two, the final level consists of n size-one leaves. Those base-case costs must be included in an exact count even though they do not change the linear-times-log bound.

With three half-size children and linear outside work, each level has one and a half times the previous level's work. A growing geometric series is controlled by its bottom levels, so the many constant-cost leaves dominate.

With two half-size children and quadratic outside work, each level has only half the previous level's work. A shrinking geometric series is controlled by its top levels, giving Θ(n²) total work.

## Depth alone is not total work

A single child on a fixed fraction of the input with constant outside work has logarithmic total cost. Changing from halves to thirds changes only a constant factor. Two half-size children with constant work per node instead create a linear number of nodes. A logarithmic depth does not imply a logarithmic total.

If one halving child does logarithmic outside work at each call, those contributions decrease gradually across the chain. Their sum is the square of a logarithm, not just one logarithm. Inspect work per level as well as depth.

## Key takeaways
- Add each level's whole cost, including base-case leaves.
- Equal level costs accumulate across the depth.
- Geometrically growing or shrinking levels favour leaves or root respectively.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)
