lessons.title: Master Theorem: leaves dominate
lessons.summary: Find the critical exponent and recognise leaf-dominated recurrences.
lessons.body:
The Master Theorem summarises the recursion-tree argument for equal-size fractional children. Use a fixed positive base-case cost and nonnegative outside work. Here n is input size.

## Compare outside work with leaf growth

```formula essential
T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
c = log_b(a)
where
T(n): total counted work on input size n
a: a fixed number of children, at least one
b: a fixed shrink divisor greater than one
f(n): work done outside the recursive calls
c: the critical exponent describing leaf-count growth
log_b: logarithm to base b
n: positive input size
In words: fixed branching and fixed fractional shrinking determine how quickly the leaf count grows; compare the parent's outside work with that leaf growth.
```

For exact full trees, take input sizes that are powers of the divisor; ordinary rounding leaves the standard asymptotic results unchanged. Leaves grow as the input raised to the critical exponent.

## When the leaves dominate

The first case requires outside work to be smaller than leaf growth by a fixed positive power of input size. A mere logarithmic difference is insufficient.

```formula essential
f(n) = O(n^{c−ε})
T(n) = Θ(n^c)
where
f(n): nonnegative outside work
n: input size
c: the critical exponent from branching and shrinking
ε: epsilon, some fixed positive exponent gap
O: an eventual upper growth bound
Θ: a tight growth bound
T(n): total work under the equal-size recurrence and fixed positive base case
In words: when outside work is polynomially smaller, the growing number of small calls determines the total growth.
```

Four half-size children produce a quadratic leaf count. Linear outside work is smaller by a full power, so the total is quadratic rather than quadratic times log.

Reducing child count can improve an algorithm's exponent. Karatsuba integer multiplication uses three half-size products instead of four, with linear outside work in digit count. Strassen matrix multiplication uses seven half-size products instead of eight, with quadratic outside work in matrix side length. Toom-3 uses five roughly third-size integer products instead of nine. These examples reduce the leaf growth; constants and representation still affect practical performance.

## Key takeaways
- Check equal fractional children and fixed parameters first.
- The critical exponent comes from branching and shrinking.
- A fixed positive power gap lets leaf growth determine the total.

## Further reading
- [MIT: Master theorem, including power gaps and regularity](https://people.csail.mit.edu/thies/6.046-web/master.pdf)
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)
- [GMP: Toom three-way multiplication](https://gmplib.org/manual/Toom-3_002dWay-Multiplication)

lessons.title: Master Theorem: balanced work
lessons.summary: Handle matching costs and logarithmic factors with the second case.
lessons.body:
When outside work matches the recursion tree's leaf growth, work is spread across many levels. The missing logarithm in a guessed answer often comes from forgetting to add those levels.

## Matching work adds a level factor

Four half-size children with quadratic outside work illustrate the idea. Each child does a quarter of the parent's outside work, but there are four children. Their combined cost matches the parent's. Every level therefore has quadratic total work, and there are logarithmically many levels. The result is Θ(n² log n), where n is the original input size.

The balanced case also has a useful logarithmic-factor extension:

```formula essential
f(n) = Θ(n^c(log(n))^k)
T(n) = Θ(n^c(log(n))^{k+1})
where
f(n): outside work in an equal-size Master Theorem recurrence
T(n): total work with bounded positive base cases
n: input size
c: the critical exponent determined by the fixed branching and shrink factors
k: a fixed nonnegative logarithm exponent
log: logarithm to a fixed base greater than one
Θ: a tight growth bound
In words: matching the critical power, possibly with a nonnegative power of a logarithm, adds one more logarithm power when work is summed across levels.
```

The exact equal-level picture applies when there is no extra logarithm factor. For two half-size children with linear-times-log outside work, the total size across a level stays the same, but the logarithm decreases gradually as subproblems shrink. Adding those declining level costs gives Θ(n(log n)²).

This is not the root-dominated case: one extra logarithm is not a fixed positive power gap. Nor does the displayed extension cover a negative logarithm exponent. Check the version of the theorem being used before applying a shortcut.

## Key takeaways
- Equal work per level must be multiplied by the number of levels.
- The nonnegative-log-power extension adds one logarithm power.
- A logarithmic factor alone is not a polynomial gap.

lessons.title: Master Theorem: root work dominates
lessons.summary: Check regularity and apply the complete three-case shortcut.
lessons.body:
The root dominates when outside work is sufficiently large and consistently shrinks down the recursion tree. Here n is input size, with fixed fractional children and bounded positive base cases.

## Larger is not enough without regularity

For the third Master Theorem case, outside work must exceed leaf growth by a fixed positive power. The children's combined outside work must also be at most a fixed fraction less than the parent's, for all sufficiently large inputs:

```formula essential
f(n) = Ω(n^{c+ε})
a f(n/b) ≤ q f(n)
T(n) = Θ(f(n))
where
f(n): nonnegative outside work
n: input size
c: the critical exponent from the recurrence's branching and shrinking
ε: a fixed positive exponent gap
a: fixed number of equal-size children
b: fixed shrink divisor greater than one
q: a fixed positive fraction strictly below one
T(n): total work
Ω: an eventual lower growth bound
Θ: a tight growth bound
≤: at most; the middle condition must hold for all sufficiently large inputs
In words: if outside work is polynomially larger than leaf growth and decreases by a fixed fraction across each generation, the root's growth determines the total.
```

Two half-size children with quadratic outside work satisfy both conditions. Each child's outside work is a quarter of the parent's, so together they cost half. Later levels keep halving. Adding all of them changes only a constant factor: total work is Θ(n²).

The regularity condition prevents a wildly varying outside-work function from hiding large costs deeper in the tree. Ordinary power functions with exponent above the critical exponent satisfy it. "Outside work looks bigger" is not a complete proof for an arbitrary function.

## The three-case picture

| Comparison with leaf growth | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Polynomially smaller | leaves dominate |
| Matching power, covered log factors | accumulate across levels |
| Polynomially larger and regular | root dominates |

Use that picture to explain the answer, then check the relevant conditions. A table of remembered recurrence answers is less reliable than understanding where the work sits.

## Key takeaways
- Root domination needs a power gap and regularity.
- Regularity makes level totals shrink geometrically.
- Explain which part of the tree supplies the dominant work.

lessons.title: When the Master Theorem does not fit
lessons.summary: Recognise unsupported recurrences and prove a guessed bound by induction.
lessons.body:
The Master Theorem is a shortcut with assumptions. When a recurrence falls outside them, inspect its actual work instead of forcing it into a case.

## Recognise the mismatch

- Subtracting one item is not shrinking by a fixed fraction. A single recursive chain with a full scan at each step has linearly many levels of decreasing linear work, giving quadratic total work.
- Two calls each one item smaller create exponential branching across a linear depth.
- Unequal-size children do not fit the equal-size theorem. Recursion trees or Akra–Bazzi may still work.
- A number of children or shrink factor that varies with input size needs a different analysis.
- Outside work smaller than the critical growth by only a logarithm falls between the leaf case and the nonnegative-log-power balanced version taught here.

For that last example, two half-size calls plus linear work divided by a logarithm give Θ(n log log n), where n is input size. The next lessons explain the slowly accumulating factor. Some stronger theorem statements cover this case directly; the limitation is in the stated version.

## Guess, then prove with the same constants

A recursion tree can suggest a bound. **Mathematical induction** then checks a base case and shows that assuming the bound for smaller inputs establishes it for the current input with the same fixed multiplier.

Here is a failed attempt for two half-size calls plus linear work:

```formula essential
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
T(n) ≤ 2c(n/2) + n = (c + 1)n
where
T(n): counted work on input size n, with a fixed positive base case
n: positive input size; use powers of two for this argument
c: the fixed multiplier in the proposed linear induction bound
≤: at most
In words: assuming a linear bound for the children produces a larger multiplier for the parent, so the proposed induction does not close.
```

Calling the final expression "linear" does not repair the proof. Repeating that multiplier increase through the levels hides the missing logarithmic factor. A linear-times-log guess has enough room for each level's added work. Its proof must cover a suitable base case; the logarithm at one is zero, so handle that size separately.

## Key takeaways
- Check the recurrence form and the growth-case conditions.
- Induction must preserve one fixed bound through every level.
- A failed proof suggests a better guess but does not prove that guess.

## Further reading
- [MIT: Master theorem, including power gaps and regularity](https://people.csail.mit.edu/thies/6.046-web/master.pdf)
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

lessons.title: Uneven splits and Akra–Bazzi
lessons.summary: Balance unequal subproblems and account for work across their scales.
lessons.body:
Unequal subproblems need not have equal depths. Akra–Bazzi extends recurrence analysis to several fixed shrinking fractions and accounts for work across those scales.

## Balance the recursive structure

Use a fixed number of positive child weights and fixed fractions strictly between zero and one. Base-case costs must stay between positive constants. Choose a sufficiently large fixed base threshold so that recursive children stay in the defined domain.

The nonnegative outside work must satisfy a polynomial-growth condition: throughout the range from each child size to its parent size, it stays between fixed positive multiples of the work at the parent size. Powers of size and logarithms used here satisfy this above a suitable threshold. Arbitrary oscillations need not. The formula below uses exact fractional sizes; rounded recurrences require the extended theorem’s conditions.

```formula essential
T(n) = g(n) + Σ_{i=1}^{m} a_i T(b_i n)
Σ_{i=1}^{m} a_i (b_i)^p = 1
where
T(n): total work on input size n
g(n): work outside the children
n: input size
m: a fixed number of child groups
i: group index
a_i: fixed positive child weight for group i
b_i: fixed fraction of parent size for group i, strictly between zero and one
p: the unique balancing exponent
Σ_{i=1}^{m}: add the expression for every group from one through m
In words: balance the weighted child-size fractions to find the recursive structure's growth before adding the outside work across scales.
```

The exact integral is reference material. An integral accumulates contributions over a continuous range, much as a sum adds contributions from discrete levels. Choose a fixed base threshold above any singularity, and use constant positive costs below it:

```formula reference
T(n) = Θ(n^p(1 + I(n)))
I(n) = ∫_{n_0}^{n} g(u)/u^{p+1} du
where
T(n): total work under the stated Akra–Bazzi assumptions
n: input size above the fixed base threshold
p: the balancing exponent
I(n): the accumulated outside-work correction
n_0: a fixed positive base threshold where the integrand is defined
g(u): outside work at size u
u: integration variable representing intermediate input size
∫: integrate over the sizes from the lower limit to the upper limit
du: integrate with respect to u
Θ: a tight growth bound
In words: start with the recursive leaf growth, then include the contribution of outside work accumulated across smaller input scales.
```

For one-third and two-thirds children with linear outside work, the pieces preserve the parent's total size. Complete early levels each cost linear work; every branch still has logarithmic depth. Total work is Θ(n log n).

For one-half and one-quarter children, total size falls to three quarters each generation. With linear outside work, this gives a shrinking geometric sum and Θ(n) total work. The root already supplies the matching linear lower bound.

## Key takeaways
- Unequal fixed fractions can still have tractable growth.
- The balancing exponent describes recursion; the correction includes outside work.
- Check regularity and base cases before applying the formula.

## Further reading
- [Leighton: Akra–Bazzi assumptions and extensions](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.046/spring04/handouts/akrabazzi.pdf)
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

Use the distribution of work to understand an Akra–Bazzi answer before evaluating an integral. Here n is the current input size, with bounded positive base cases.

## Selection: leave a fixed fraction out

Median-of-medians selection groups items into fives, recursively finds a pivot from the group medians, then recurses only into the relevant partition. Its worst-case analysis bounds child sizes by about one fifth and seven tenths of the parent, with rounding and a constant-sized boundary correction. This is an upper-bound recurrence for the algorithm, not an exact equality for every input.

Those fractions total less than the whole input. With linear partitioning work, the recursive contribution shrinks geometrically once inputs are large enough. The resulting worst-case bound is linear. The small rounding corrections are handled by the base threshold; they do not remove the fixed gap below the full parent size.

## A logarithmic gap accumulates slowly

Consider this recurrence for sufficiently large inputs, stopping at a fixed size above one:

```formula essential
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/log_2(n)
T(n) = Θ(n log_2(log_2(n)))
where
T(n): total work, with bounded positive cost below the fixed base threshold
n: input size; use powers of two to visualise the levels
log_2: base-two logarithm; the outer logarithm is applied to the inner result
Θ: a tight growth bound
In words: outside work slightly below linear still accumulates across the tree, adding a slowly growing log-log factor to the linear leaf cost.
```

Each complete level contains the same total item count, but its outside work is divided by the logarithm of the current subproblem size. Looking upward from the base, those denominators grow in roughly consecutive steps. The level contributions therefore form a harmonic sum over logarithmically many levels. That adds the logarithm of a logarithm.

The result lies between linear and linear-times-log growth. It is not covered by the nonnegative-log-power balanced case or the leaf case requiring a fixed positive power gap. Akra–Bazzi's accumulated outside-work correction distinguishes it without pretending those conditions hold.

## Key takeaways
- A fixed gap below the parent size can support linear selection.
- Real algorithm recurrences may be upper bounds with rounding corrections.
- Slightly sublinear outside work can still add a growing factor across levels.

## Further reading
- [Erickson: Solving Recurrences](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/notes/99-recurrences.pdf)

lessons.title: Estimating a feasible input budget
lessons.summary: Use an explicitly assumed operation rate to screen algorithm choices.
lessons.body:
Complexity helps reject implausible designs before implementing them. It does not supply a universal number of operations a machine can perform each second.

## Build a workload-specific budget

Start with the largest expected input, the actual operation being counted and the time available. A comparison of two small integers is different from a network request or comparison of long strings. Use measured throughput for representative data, or label a hypothetical rate clearly.

| Candidate | What to investigate |
|---|---|
| All pairs | whether quadratic growth fits the largest input |
| Sort then scan | comparison cost, allocation and input mutation |
| Hash-based scan | memory, hash quality and equality cost |
| Exhaustive subsets | candidate count and cost of checking each |

A quadratic design can look fine on a sample and fail when an upload grows substantially. Sorting or hashing may avoid most of those comparisons. Conversely, exhaustive search can be the simplest exact solution for a tightly bounded small input. There is no universal "twenty to twenty-five items" limit: pruning, per-candidate work, parallelism and the time budget alter feasibility.

## Treat an estimate as a model to validate

Dividing counted work by a representative operations-per-second rate gives an estimated runtime. A range of observed rates produces a range of predicted times. Do not substitute CPU clock frequency for measured iteration throughput.

If the larger input crosses a cache or memory boundary, the old rate may no longer apply. Include allocation, parsing, output and peak memory when those are part of the job. Leave headroom instead of relying on a model that only just fits.

Big-O is an upper growth bound with hidden constants, not an exact operation count. A label alone cannot justify a particular one-second deadline. Use the mechanism to screen candidates, then benchmark the actual implementation and workload.

## Key takeaways
- Feasibility depends on input bounds, operation cost and available time.
- Exhaustive search has no universal practical item cutoff.
- Use estimates to choose what to measure, not to replace measurement.

## Further reading
- [Python timeit](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/timeit.html)
- [Erickson: Introduction](https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/teaching/algorithms/book/00-intro.pdf)

lessons.title: Constants, locality and theoretical winners
lessons.summary: Explain practical performance differences hidden by asymptotic labels.
lessons.body:
Two implementations can share a growth class yet perform very differently. Asymptotic notation deliberately hides fixed factors and simplifies the memory system.

## Small pieces can favour simple methods

Insertion sort has quadratic worst-case work in its run length, but small pieces can benefit from its simple operations and contiguous access. A hybrid sort can use it only below a fixed run-size cap. Across all pieces, that bounded work remains linear in the total item count; the merging or partitioning stages determine the larger-input bound.

CPython 3.14's natural merge sort extends short runs using binary insertion sort and uses a Powersort merge policy. Its tuning choices are implementation details. The useful general idea is to bound expensive small-run work and measure whether it helps.

## Locality changes the cost per access

Contiguous arrays place neighbouring values near one another. Scattered linked-list nodes require following references; the next address may not be known until the previous node is loaded. Both traversals are linear in item count, but their cache misses and memory dependencies differ.

For a C-style row-major matrix, neighbouring columns within one row are contiguous. Traversing down a column instead jumps by a row stride. Both orders visit every entry, yet row order usually has better spatial locality for large matrices. Exact timing depends on layout, cache size, associativity, compiler transformations and hardware. Total matrix size alone does not prove every column access misses the cache.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Reading a shelf in order
> Reading adjacent book labels can be easier than following instructions to shelves across a building.
>
> **How it maps:** Nearby array elements resemble adjacent labels; dependent pointers resemble directions learned only after reaching each location.
>
> **Where it stops:** CPUs prefetch, cache and overlap work. The comparison suggests locality, not a numerical slowdown.

## A smaller exponent still needs a practical implementation

Some theoretically faster algorithms have large constants or extra storage needs. Compare a proposed matrix-multiplication implementation with a measured baseline using representative sizes, numeric types, memory limits and accuracy requirements. A ratio of powers with assumed unit constants cannot establish a real speedup.

## Key takeaways
- Constants and locality matter over finite input ranges.
- A bounded quadratic subroutine can fit inside a faster-growing overall algorithm.
- Benchmark time, peak memory and accuracy before replacing a tuned baseline.

## Further reading
- [CPython 3.14 sorting design](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/3.14/Objects/listsort.txt)
- [What every programmer should know about memory](https://www.akkadia.org/drepper/cpumemory.pdf)

questions.prompt: On a target machine with 64-byte cache lines, an array traversal benchmarks faster than traversing a linked list whose nodes are scattered across the heap. Both sum the same n integers in Θ(n) time (time proportional to n). What explains a possible gap?

options.text: The array has contiguous access and spatial locality; the list follows dependent pointers that may miss in cache
options.explanation: Correct. The next node address depends on loading the current node. This serial dependency and poor spatial locality can make scattered traversal slower; exact latency requires target-specific measurement.

options.text: Linked lists are Θ(n log n) to traverse because of pointer overhead
options.explanation: Traversal is still Θ(n), proportional to the number of nodes n: one step per node. The difference is in the constant factor per step, not the growth rate. Here n is the input item count.

options.text: The compiler can't optimise linked list code at all
options.explanation: Compilers can optimise both. The dependent memory accesses in the specified scattered list remain a possible bottleneck; the claim that no optimisation is possible is too strong.

options.text: Linked lists store more data, so there's more to add up
options.explanation: The values added are the same. The extra pointer per node increases memory traffic a bit, but the main cost is latency from scattered, dependent accesses.

questions.workedExample: A contiguous array lets nearby accesses reuse cache lines. Scattered list traversal also depends on loading each next pointer before knowing the following address. Both visit n values, so both are linear, but the cost per visit can differ. Measure the target workload; the explanation does not establish a universal speed ratio.

options.text: B, because it accesses columns, which are stored contiguously in C
options.explanation: C multidimensional arrays store complete rows consecutively; the column direction is not contiguous.

options.text: Neither: both are Θ(N^2) and do the same additions
options.explanation: The loops have the same Θ(N^2) work and arithmetic but different access patterns; N is side length. Asymptotic growth does not capture locality.

options.text: A walks adjacent entries; B jumps by a full row stride
options.explanation: Correct. The column index selects adjacent elements within a row. Changing row while holding column fixed jumps across rows.

options.text: A, because it has fewer loop iterations
options.explanation: Both visit every cell exactly once. The difference is the cost of memory accesses.

Both loops visit the same number of cells, but A has better sequential locality. Cache reuse across later columns depends on cache capacity and associativity, so measure the speed difference.

questions.prompt: Consider a natural merge sort on n items that uses binary insertion sort to extend short runs to a bounded target of at most 64 elements. Why can this quadratic subroutine fit an O(n log n) overall sort?

options.text: Because insertion sort is Θ(n) on every input
options.explanation: The worst-case moving cost is still quadratic in run length. Binary search reduces position-finding comparisons, not the number of elements that may need to shift.

options.text: Because insertion sort uses less memory than merge sort for large n
options.explanation: It's true insertion sort is in place, but that's not why it's used here. It's chosen for speed on small pieces.

options.text: To guarantee stability, which merge sort can't provide
options.explanation: Merge sort is stable, and so is Timsort's merge step. Stability isn't the reason.

options.text: A fixed cap bounds the small-run cost, so total extension work stays linear
options.explanation: Correct. The bounded run length caps the quadratic subroutine at a fixed cost; distributing such runs across the item count gives linear total extension work. Small-run constants make it worthwhile.

questions.workedExample: The short-run cap is a fixed constant, independent of total input length n. Quadratic work on each capped run is bounded by a constant times that run’s length. Summed across all runs, extension work is linear; the merge stage can retain O(n log n) overall time. The cap and practical crossover are implementation choices.

options.text: Keep the existing baseline until representative benchmarks show that the proposed implementation is faster and meets memory and accuracy needs
options.explanation: Correct. A smaller exponent alone does not establish performance for a particular matrix workload. Constants, implementation, memory and numerical behaviour matter.

options.text: Adopt it immediately because its exponent is smaller
options.explanation: A smaller exponent does not quantify finite-size time without constants, implementation and workload details.

options.text: Adopt it only for square matrices, since the exponent only applies to them
options.explanation: Input shape matters for benchmarking, but squareness alone does not establish a performance benefit.

options.text: Use Strassen's algorithm instead, since it is always faster than Θ(n^3)
options.explanation: Strassen is not universally faster. Its extra work, memory use and numerical behaviour require evaluation for the target workload.

Require an actual implementation and benchmark representative shapes and numeric types. Compare peak memory and numerical accuracy as well as elapsed time. Keep the existing measured baseline until the alternative demonstrates the needed improvement.

questions.prompt: Which factors can explain why a Θ(n²) algorithm beats a Θ(n log n) algorithm over a particular finite input range? Here n is the input size, log denotes its base-2 logarithm. Select all that apply. Let A be Θ(n log n) and B be Θ(n²).

options.text: Inputs are always tiny, say at most 30 items
options.explanation: Yes. Below the crossover point the asymptotic class doesn't decide anything; a simple quadratic loop with tiny constants often wins. This is why sorting libraries use insertion sort for small pieces.

options.text: A chases pointers through scattered heap nodes, while B scans a contiguous array
options.explanation: Yes. Dependent cache misses can inflate A’s measured cost per operation. Exact latency depends on hardware and workload.

options.text: A's constant factor is hundreds of times larger than B's
options.explanation: Yes. A much larger coefficient can let the faster-growing quadratic model win over a finite range. Measure the range relevant to the workload.

options.text: Larger n alone guarantees that the quadratic algorithm wins
options.explanation: False. Slower asymptotic growth wins eventually, but no finite crossover is implied without constants.

options.text: Both are written in the same programming language
options.explanation: A shared language does not by itself favour either implementation. Their operations and representations can still differ.

questions.workedExample: Finite-range performance includes constants, allocation and access patterns. Small inputs, expensive dependent memory accesses in A, or a much larger coefficient in A can let B win. Larger input alone eventually favours A’s slower growth under fixed comparable cost models. Sharing a language does not determine the winner.

lessons.title: Hostile inputs and worst-case bounds
lessons.summary: Recognise when an attacker can force expensive algorithm paths.
lessons.body:
Typical performance is not enough when someone can choose inputs that expose expensive paths. Ask what the algorithm guarantees under the actual input and randomness model.

## Three ways input can amplify work

- **Hash collisions:** a basic hash table can degrade to a linear scan when many keys collide. Repeated insertion can then take quadratic work in the key count. Keyed hash randomisation makes predictable collision attacks harder; it is not a universal constant-time guarantee for arbitrary keys.
- **Regex backtracking:** some patterns force a backtracking engine to explore many alternatives, giving superlinear or exponential behaviour. Cloudflare's July 2019 outage involved excessive backtracking that exhausted CPU capacity. Check the engine and the exact search API: guarantees for one fixed-pattern search do not automatically cover repeated-match iteration or an unbounded pattern size.
- **Predictable quicksort pivots:** repeatedly selecting an end element on sorted distinct input leaves one nearly unchanged partition and can cause quadratic work. Randomisation gives an expected guarantee under its assumptions; an introspective fallback to heapsort supplies a worst-case time bound.

## Match the defence to the source of risk

Use a suitable worst-case bound when latency must be bounded by the algorithm. Where randomisation is appropriate, state what remains unpredictable to the input chooser. Apply input and resource limits as well: even a linear scan takes too long or too much memory on an unbounded request.

A fixed tiny configuration list and an ordinary fixed-width numeric sum do not have the same shape-dependent amplification as those examples. That does not make all costs irrelevant: huge input, expensive user-defined comparisons or growing integers require their own model.

## Key takeaways
- Check who chooses the input and which slow paths remain reachable.
- Randomised expected guarantees and worst-case guarantees are different.
- Bound input size and operation cost as well as the growth rate.

## Further reading
- [Python hash randomisation](https://docs.python.org/3.14/reference/datamodel.html#object.__hash__)
- [Cloudflare's July 2019 outage analysis](https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/)
- [RE2 design guarantees](https://github.com/google/re2)

questions.prompt: In which of these situations should you design for the **worst case** because the input could be adversarial? Select all that apply. For the simple sum, assume fixed-width numbers and ordinary constant-cost addition.

options.text: A public web API stores request parameters in a hash table keyed by attacker-supplied strings
options.explanation: Yes. Predictable hash collisions can make each insertion linear and the whole insertion sequence quadratic in key count, as in the 2011 hash-flooding attacks. Keyed randomised hashing defends against that pattern; n is key count.

options.text: A web application firewall runs a backtracking regular expression over every incoming request
options.explanation: Yes. Backtracking can be superlinear or exponential depending on the pattern, input and engine. Cloudflare's July 2019 incident showed how excessive backtracking can exhaust CPU capacity.

options.text: A script sorts a fixed list of 12 configuration entries at start-up
options.explanation: This is a fixed tiny input controlled by the application; it lacks attacker-selected growth. Its actual startup cost can still be measured.

options.text: A service sorts user-uploaded files with a quicksort that always picks the first element as pivot
options.explanation: Yes. Already sorted uploads can trigger quadratic quicksort behaviour with a poor predictable pivot. Use a stated randomisation model or a library sort with a worst-case bound; n is item count.

options.text: An internal batch job sums the values in a list
options.explanation: Under the stated fixed-width model, value order does not cause a superlinear path. Input length still needs a practical bound.

questions.workedExample: Look for input-controlled amplification: colliding hash keys, costly backtracking and repeatedly unbalanced quicksort partitions. A fixed tiny controlled list lacks that growth opportunity. A fixed-width sum scans once regardless of value order, although huge input or expensive arithmetic still needs bounds. Match worst-case or randomised guarantees to the workload.

lessons.title: Measuring and choosing an algorithm
lessons.summary: Use doubling ratios and realistic constraints to choose a suitable implementation.
lessons.body:
Measurement tests whether the model explains the actual implementation. Use realistic inputs, repeat runs and inspect the operations dominating elapsed time.

## Doubling is a diagnostic experiment

Measure at several successively doubled input sizes while holding the task and environment comparable. A roughly doubled time suggests linear behaviour; quadrupled time suggests quadratic behaviour; eightfold time suggests cubic behaviour. Linear-times-log growth is slightly above doubling over sufficiently large sizes.

These are clues over the measured range, not proofs of asymptotic bounds. Startup work, cache transitions, allocation and noise can distort ratios. A backtracking or exponential algorithm need not follow a stable power-law ratio at all.

Python's `timeit` repeats small benchmarks and documents common measurement pitfalls. Decide whether setup and garbage collection belong in the measured workload. Minimum repeated time can help estimate uncontended execution; service latency needs its own distribution, including slow requests. A profiler identifies where time is spent but also adds overhead.

## Connect the observation to the code

```python
def drain(items):
    out = []
    while items:
        out.append(items.pop(0))
    return out
```

One visible loop does not make this linear. Each front removal shifts the remaining list references, so the total work is quadratic in original item count. A consistent fourfold doubling ratio supports that diagnosis. A deque can remove from the front without shifting every remaining element. Copying once and clearing the original may also satisfy the required behaviour; check mutation and aliasing requirements.

## Choose for the scarce resource

To keep the best hundred scores from a stream too large to store, maintain a min-heap of at most a hundred retained scores. Its smallest retained score is the replacement threshold. Read every record once and replace only when necessary. Storage depends on the requested result count, not stream length.

A conventional in-memory quickselect requires the items available for partitioning, and sorting all records does more ordering than the request needs. Match the approach to output, memory and streaming requirements, then benchmark it.

## Key takeaways
- Doubling ratios suggest where to investigate.
- Confirm the mechanism behind an observed slowdown.
- Choose and measure against actual input, output, memory and latency constraints.

## Further reading
- [Python timeit](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/timeit.html)
- [Python heap selection](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/heapq.html)
- [Python deque](https://docs.python.org/3.14/library/collections.html)

questions.prompt: You time a function at input sizes 1,000, 2,000 and 4,000 and get 0.1 s, 0.8 s and 6.4 s. What complexity does this suggest? Here n is item count.

options.text: O(n)
options.explanation: Linear would double the time when n doubles. Here it goes up 8-fold.
Correct. Each doubling multiplies observed time eightfold, suggesting exponent three over that range.
Quadratic would give a ratio of 4 per doubling (0.1, 0.4, 1.6). The measured ratio is 8.
A base-two exponential would gain a thousand extra powers when input grows from one thousand to two thousand, far more than the observed ratio.

questions.workedExample: Each input doubling has an observed eightfold time increase, which suggests cubic growth over that range. It is evidence to investigate, not proof for all sizes. Repeat representative measurements and inspect the code; setup, cache changes or other effects can distort scaling.

questions.prompt:
This function is documented as 'linear'. You time it at 50,000, 100,000 and 200,000 items and get 0.3 s, 1.2 s and 4.8 s. What is the most likely cause?

```python
def drain(items):
    out = []
    while items:
        # Front removal shifts items.
        out.append(items.pop(0))
    # Empty items; out keeps its order.
    return out
```

Here n is the item count.

options.text: Python's `append` is O(n), so building `out` is quadratic
options.explanation: `append` is O(1) amortised. Building the output list is linear.

options.text: The timings are noise; a ratio of 4 is close enough to 2
options.explanation: Repeated fourfold ratios support investigating quadratic work, though timings alone are not a proof. The front-removal mechanism provides the explanation here.

options.text: The garbage collector runs more often for larger lists, which is linear overhead
options.explanation: Runtime effects can affect measurements, but the explicit repeated shifting already explains quadratic work. It should be addressed before attributing the pattern to garbage collection.

options.text: `items.pop(0)` shifts all remaining elements each time, so the loop is Θ(n^2); use `collections.deque.popleft()` or iterate directly
options.explanation: Correct. Every front removal shifts the remaining items, and summing those shrinking counts gives quadratic work. The measured fourfold doubling ratio supports that diagnosis. A deque provides constant-time front removal; n is original list length.

questions.workedExample: Each front removal shifts all remaining list references. Adding those decreasing lengths gives quadratic work in initial item count n, consistent with the observed fourfold doubling ratios. A deque avoids the shifts; copying once and clearing the original may also fit, depending on required mutation and aliasing behaviour.

questions.prompt: You need the **100 highest scores** from a stream of one billion records, on a machine that can't hold the whole dataset in memory. Which approach is best? Here n is record count.

options.text: Load everything into a list and sort it: O(n log n)
options.explanation: The data doesn't fit in memory, and even if it did, sorting does far more work than needed: it orders all 10^9 records when you only need 100.

options.text: Quickselect for the 100th largest, then filter: O(n) average
options.explanation: Conventional in-memory quickselect partitions a resident collection. It does not directly satisfy the one-pass stream and bounded-memory requirement in this scenario.

options.text: Keep a min-heap of size 100 while streaming: O(n log 100) time, O(100) memory
options.explanation: Correct. Compare each score with the retained minimum; replacements need logarithmic work in the fixed heap size. Its roughly seven tree levels are not an exact comparison count.

options.text: Compare each record against every record already seen
options.explanation: Pairwise search is quadratic and requires retaining the input, violating the streaming memory constraint.

questions.workedExample: Retain only the best hundred seen so far in a min-heap. Its minimum is the threshold for replacing a retained score. Each record needs a threshold check and at most logarithmic work in the fixed retained count. This supports one-pass processing with bounded storage. Conventional in-memory sorting and quickselect require access to the full collection.
